Q: "Deadlock" caused by virtual threads in JDK21 A:

The deadlock occurs in Java 21 when using two carrier threads (fixed in JDK 24 by https://openjdk.org/jeps/491):

  1. VirtualThread-A acquires a ReentrantLock outside a synchronized block.

  2. VirtualThread-A does I/O and get unmounted of carrier thread while still holding the lock.

  3. VirtualThread-B and VirtualThread-C inside a synchronized block tries to acquire the same lock.

Both carrier threads now hold pinned virtual threads (B and C) and cannot unmount them because they're in synchronized blocks. VirtualThread-B and VirtualThread-C enter WAITING state waiting for the lock or the monitor of synchronized. VirtualThread-A becomes RUNNABLE and ready to continue, but no carrier thread is available to run it because both are pinned by threads B and C.

In your code, the lock acquisition is hidden inside System.out.printf(). PrintStream uses a ReentrantLock internally. When one virtual thread calls printf() outside a synchronized block and gets unmounted during I/O, other virtual threads calling synchonized or printf() inside synchronized blocks get pinned while waiting for that same lock or the monitor lock, exhausting all carrier threads.

Notes:
- In Java 21, a virtual thread becomes pinned to its carrier thread as soon as it calls synchronized and begins waiting to acquire the monitor lock, not just after acquiring it.
- Some libraries might implement a combination of Lock and synchronized calls leading to deadlocks when called by virtual threads. For example Apache httpClient 4.X, see https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/HTTPCORE-746

If you plan to use virtual thread consider to use Java JVM >=24 as synchronized is not pinning to carrier, thus avoiding carrier threads exhaustion leading to deadlocks.

Q: How to call a PostgreSQL bulk upsert function in TypeScript/BunJS A:

Postgres can't cast json or json[] to response_input[] directly, but there's a json_populate_recordset() that can handle a native json array (a single PostgreSQL json-type value with a native JSON array in it:

json_populate_recordset ( base anyelement, from_json json ) → setof anyelement
Expands the top-level JSON array of objects to a set of rows having the composite type of the base argument.

To handle a json[], a SQL array with multipel separate json values in it, you can unnest it first, then convert each element with json_populate_record(), a scalar variant of the set-returning function above. After converting, re-aggregate the results back into a response_input[] you wanted, with an array() constructor.

  const result = await sql` 
  SELECT * 
  FROM upsert_responses_bulk(
         array(SELECT json_populate_record(null::response_input,e) 
               FROM unnest(${sql.array(tuples)}) AS unpacked(e)
         )
       );`

Here's some examples using a json-type value, with a native JSON array in it:

Q: Window is smaller than requested in CreateWindowExW() A:

This is a classic, well-known issue.

In fact, when you call CreateWindowExW, the position and size parameters

CW_USEDEFAULT,
CW_USEDEFAULT,
300,
100,

refer to the window size including the non-client area (borders, title bar, etc.).

If you want the client area to be exactly 300×100, you must first calculate the total window size including the borders.
That is exactly what AdjustWindowRectEx is for.

DWORD style = WS_OVERLAPPED | WS_CAPTION | WS_SYSMENU;
RECT rc = { 0, 0, 300, 100 };
AdjustWindowRectEx(&rc, style, FALSE, 0);

The code above means: under the specified window style, compute the actual window rectangle required to get a client area from (0,0) to (300,100).
AdjustWindowRectEx modifies rc in place, so you can then compute:

int winWidth  = rc.right - rc.left;
int winHeight = rc.bottom - rc.top;
int borderLeft = -rc.left;

Then create the window like this:

HWND hwnd = CreateWindowExW(
    0,
    WndClassName,
    L"300 x 100 window",
    style,
    -borderLeft,
    0,
    winWidth,
    winHeight,
    NULL,
    NULL,
    hInstance,
    NULL
);

Now the client area will be exactly 300×100 as expected.

Q: Removing $null or Blanks from CSV Results A:

To complement iRon's helpful answer with a more concise and performant alternative:

$values = 
  [array] $testCsv.$header -ne ''

That is:

  • In lieu of Select-Object -ExpandProperty, member-access enumeration is used to extract all the values of the column named in $header.

  • The [array] cast ensures that the result is always treated as an array (if there happened to be just one data row, a single value rather than an array would be returned).

  • -ne, the inequality operator is then used to filter out all empty-string ('') values, taking advantage of the common feature of PowerShell's comparison operators that makes them act as filters with an array as their LHS, i.e. only to return the subarray of those array elements for which the comparison is true.

Q: How do executables being part of the same application find eachother on MS Windows? A:

The normal way to do this is simply to have the binaries in the same directory. The program name can be predictable, but the directory it's installed in is never predictable.

It can be found here: How do I find the location of the executable in C?

Even on Linux/Unix you never hard-code the path into the executable.

On MS Windows you can find the program directory using GetModuleFileName as described here: How to get the program path i am executing with "open with" method?
